In [[applied mathematics]], the '''Atkinson–Mingarelli theorem''', named after [[Frederick Valentine Atkinson]] and A. B. Mingarelli, concerns eigenvalues of certain [[Sturm–Liouville]] [[differential operator]]s.

In the simplest of formulations let ''p'', ''q'', ''w'' be real-valued [[piecewise continuous]] functions defined on a closed bounded real interval, {{math|1=''I'' = [''a'', ''b'']}}. The function ''w''(''x''), which is sometimes denoted by ''r''(''x''), is called the "weight" or "density" function. Consider the [[Sturm–Liouville]] differential equation

{{NumBlk|:|<math> -\frac{d}{dx}\left[p(x)\frac{dy}{ dx}\right]+q(x)y=\lambda w(x)y,</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

where ''y'' is a function of the independent variable ''x''. In this case, ''y'' is called a ''solution'' if it is continuously differentiable on (''a'',''b'') and (''p'' ''y''′)(''x'') is piecewise continuously differentiable and ''y'' satisfies the equation ({{EquationNote|1}}) at all except a finite number of points in (''a'',''b''). The unknown function ''y'' is typically required to satisfy some [[boundary condition]]s at ''a'' and ''b''.

The boundary conditions under consideration here are usually called [[separated boundary conditions]] and they are of the form:

{{NumBlk|:|<math> \alpha_{1}y(a)+\alpha_{2}y'(a)=0\qquad(\alpha_1^2+\alpha_2^2>0),</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

{{NumBlk|:|<math> \beta_{1}y(b)+\beta_{2}y'(b)=0\qquad(\beta_1^2+\beta_2^2>0),</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}

where the <math> \{\alpha_i, \beta_i\}</math>, {{math|1=''i'' = 1, 2}} are real numbers. We define

== The theorem ==

Assume that ''p''(''x'') has a finite number of sign changes and that the positive (resp. negative) part of the function ''p''(''x'')/''w''(''x'') defined by <math>(w/p)_{+}(x) = \max \{w(x)/p(x), 0\}</math>, (resp. <math>(w/p)_{-}(x) = \max \{ -w(x)/p(x), 0\})</math> are not identically zero  functions over I. Then the eigenvalue problem ({{EquationNote|1}}), ({{EquationNote|2}})–({{EquationNote|3}}) has an infinite number of real positive eigenvalues <math>{\lambda_i}^{+}</math>,
<math display="block"> 0 < {\lambda_1}^{+} < {\lambda_2}^{+} < {\lambda_3}^{+} < \cdots < {\lambda_n}^{+} < \cdots \to \infty; </math>
and an infinite number of negative eigenvalues <math>{\lambda_i}^{-}</math>,
<math display="block"> 0 > {\lambda_1}^{-} > {\lambda_2}^{-} > {\lambda_3}^{-} > \cdots > {\lambda_n}^{-} > \cdots \to - \infty; </math>
whose spectral asymptotics are given by their solution [2] of Jörgens' Conjecture [3]:
<math display="block"> {\lambda_n}^{+} \sim \frac{n^2 \pi^2}{\left(\int_a^b \sqrt{(w/p)_{+}(x)}\, dx\right)^2},\quad n \to \infty, </math>
and
<math display="block"> {\lambda_n}^{-} \sim \frac{- n^2 \pi^2}{\left(\int_a^b \sqrt{(w/p)_{-}(x)}\, dx\right)^2},\quad n \to \infty. </math>

For more information on the general theory behind ({{EquationNote|1}}) see the article on [[Sturm–Liouville theory]]. The stated theorem is actually valid more generally for coefficient functions <math>1/p,\, q,\, w</math> that are [[Lebesgue integrable]] over {{mvar|I}}.
